children.title: Macromolecules & Enzymes
children.description: The four macromolecule classes, their monomers and jobs, and how enzymes speed reactions until heat or pH bends them out of shape.

children.title: Carbohydrates
children.description: Sugars and their polymers: the cell's quick-energy and structural molecule.

teach.headline: Sugars Build Carbohydrates
teach.body:
Carbohydrates are made of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. Their monomer is the **monosaccharide** — a single sugar like glucose.

Link monosaccharides into chains and you get polymers: **starch** and **glycogen** store energy, while **cellulose** builds rigid plant cell walls. So the same sugar building block does double duty — fast fuel and structure.
teach.mnemonic: MONO = ONE. SACCHAR = SUGAR. ONE sugar is a monosaccharide; chain many for starch.
teach.poweredIdea: Carbohydrates are polymers of monosaccharides used for quick energy and structure.

data.prompt: The monomer (building block) of a carbohydrate is a _____.
data.hint: A single sugar unit, like glucose

data.story: A runner eats a banana right before a sprint and feels a quick burst of usable energy.
data.question: Which macromolecule is the runner relying on for that fast energy?
data.explanation: Carbohydrates like the sugars in fruit are broken down quickly for readily available energy.

achievement.flavor: You trace single sugars chaining into starch for fuel and cellulose for structure.

children.authorNotes: NC LS.Bio.1.1 (macromolecule structure/function). Concepts align with the 2025 Biology EOC macromolecule items; text and quizzes original. Does not reuse biochem.* ids.

children.title: Lipids
children.description: Fats, oils, and phospholipids: long-term energy and the cell membrane.

teach.headline: Lipids Store Energy and Build Membranes
teach.body:
Lipids are not built from a single repeating monomer the way the other classes are. Most are assembled from **fatty acids** and **glycerol**, and they are water-fearing (hydrophobic).

Their jobs: long-term energy storage, insulation, and — critically — the **phospholipid** bilayer that forms every cell membrane.
teach.mnemonic: LIP = FAT. Lipids are FATS and oils — water-fearing energy stores that build membranes.
teach.poweredIdea: Lipids store long-term energy and form the phospholipid cell membrane.

data.prompt: The cell membrane is built mainly from a type of lipid called a _____.
data.hint: Phosphate-headed lipid that forms a bilayer

data.story: A bear packs on body fat through autumn so it can survive months of winter hibernation without eating.
data.question: Which macromolecule is the bear storing for long-term energy?
data.explanation: Lipids pack the most energy per gram, making them ideal for long-term storage.

achievement.flavor: You see why water-fearing fats store dense energy and line up into the cell membrane.

children.authorNotes: NC LS.Bio.1.1 (macromolecule structure/function). Original text and quizzes; no biochem.* id reuse.

children.title: Proteins
children.description: Amino-acid chains that fold into shapes; shape decides the job.

teach.headline: Amino Acids Fold Into Proteins
teach.body:
Proteins are chains of **amino acids** (20 kinds). The order of amino acids makes the chain fold into a precise 3D **shape**, and that shape determines what the protein does.

Proteins build structures, transport materials, defend as antibodies, and act as enzymes. Change the shape — by heat or pH — and the protein stops working.
teach.mnemonic: SHAPE = FUNCTION. Amino acids fold; the FOLD does the job. Unfold it and the protein quits.
teach.poweredIdea: Proteins are amino-acid chains whose folded shape determines their function.

data.prompt: The monomer (building block) of a protein is an _____.
data.hint: Twenty kinds chain together to make proteins

data.story: A clear egg white turns solid and white when fried. The amino-acid sequence has not changed, but the egg can never go back to liquid.
data.question: What happened to the proteins in the egg white?
data.answer: Heat changed their shape (denatured them), so they no longer function as before.
options: Heat changed their shape (denatured them), so they no longer function as before.
Heat changed their amino-acid sequence into a new protein.
Heat turned the proteins into carbohydrates.
Heat added more amino acids to each protein.
data.explanation: Denaturation unfolds a protein's 3D shape without changing its amino-acid order — and shape is what determines function.

achievement.flavor: You connect amino-acid order to folded shape and shape to the protein's job.

children.authorNotes: NC LS.Bio.1.1. Sets up shape/denaturation for the enzyme drawer. Original content; no biochem.* id reuse.

children.title: Nucleic Acids (DNA & RNA)
children.description: Nucleotide chains that store and carry genetic information.

teach.headline: Nucleotides Build DNA and RNA
teach.body:
The monomer of a nucleic acid is the **nucleotide** — a sugar, a phosphate, and a nitrogen base.

**DNA** is double-stranded, with alternating **deoxyribose** and **phosphate** groups forming the two sides and the bases **A, G, C, T** paired down the middle. **RNA** is single-stranded, uses **ribose** instead of deoxyribose, and swaps thymine for **uracil (U)**.
teach.mnemonic: DNA = DEOXYRIBOSE + ThYMINE. RNA = RIBOSE + URACIL. Drop one oxygen, swap one base.
teach.poweredIdea: DNA is a double helix of nucleotides: deoxyribose-phosphate sides with A-G-C-T bases inside.

data.prompt: In DNA, the two sides alternate between the sugar deoxyribose and _____ groups.
data.hint: The other half of the sugar-_____ backbone

data.paragraph: DNA is a single-stranded molecule with a ribose-and-phosphate backbone and the bases adenine, guanine, cytosine, and uracil running down the middle.
data.bugPhrase: single-stranded molecule with a ribose-and-phosphate backbone and the bases adenine, guanine, cytosine, and uracil
data.hint: Which features belong to RNA, not DNA?
data.canonicalFix: DNA is double-stranded with a deoxyribose-and-phosphate backbone, and its bases are adenine, guanine, cytosine, and thymine. Ribose and uracil belong to RNA.
data.poweredIdea: DNA uses deoxyribose and thymine and is double-stranded; ribose and uracil are RNA's.

data.mnemonic: DEOXY = MISSING OXYGEN. DNA's sugar is DEOXYribose — RNA keeps the oxygen in plain ribose.

question.prompt: Which sugar forms the backbone of DNA?

achievement.flavor: You keep DNA and RNA straight: deoxyribose and thymine versus ribose and uracil.

children.authorNotes: NC LS.Bio.1.1. Maps to the DNA-structure item (released #1); the debug-the-claim targets the ribose/uracil distractor trap. Reworded, not reproduced. No biochem.* id reuse.

children.title: Enzymes & Reaction Rate
children.description: Protein catalysts that speed reactions, work on specific substrates, and denature outside their optimal conditions.

teach.headline: Enzymes Speed Reactions, Never Used Up
teach.body:
An **enzyme** is a protein **catalyst**: it lowers the activation energy a reaction needs and speeds it up, yet the enzyme itself is not consumed and can be reused. Each enzyme fits a specific **substrate** like a key in a lock.

Adding more enzyme speeds the reaction as long as substrate is available. But every enzyme has an **optimal** temperature and pH. Move toward that optimum and the rate rises; go past it and the enzyme **denatures** — its shape changes and it stops working.

![Enzyme-substrate complex with active site, substrate, and products](/content/bio-eoc/figures/bio_eoc_enzyme_substrate.svg)

figures.alt: Enzyme-substrate complex diagram labeling the active site, substrate, and products
figures.caption: The substrate binds at the enzyme's active site; products are released unchanged enzyme.

teach.mnemonic: SHAPE DOES THE WORK. Too hot and the enzyme DENATURES — wrong shape, no reaction.
teach.poweredIdea: Enzymes are protein catalysts that lower activation energy; denaturing their shape stops them.

data.prompt: A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up is a _____.
In the diagram, the substrate binds at the enzyme's _____.
data.hint: The shaped pocket where the substrate fits

data.story: Enzyme X is required for a reaction, and there is plenty of substrate available. A researcher adds extra Enzyme X to the mixture.
data.question: What is the most likely result?
data.answer: An increase in the reaction rate
options: An increase in the reaction rate
A decrease in the reaction rate
A decrease in the product concentration
An increase in the substrate concentration
data.explanation: With substrate still available, more enzyme means more reactions happening at once, so the rate goes up.

data.scenario: Hydrogen peroxide poured on a slice of raw potato bubbles vigorously as catalase breaks it into water and oxygen. When the same is poured on a slice of potato that was boiled first, nothing happens.
data.predictPrompt: Why does the boiled potato show no reaction?
predictOptions: Heating made the peroxide evaporate before it could react
Heat changed the shape of the catalase enzyme, so it can no longer function
Heating released the water and oxygen ahead of time
Heating had no effect; the potato simply ran out of peroxide
data.runNarrative: Boiling denatured the catalase. Its active site no longer fits hydrogen peroxide, so the enzyme cannot catalyze the breakdown — no bubbles. The raw potato's catalase still has its shape, so it works.
data.truthSummary: High heat denatures an enzyme by changing its 3D shape; a misshapen enzyme cannot bind its substrate.

bugCandidates.label: I said the heat made the peroxide evaporate or escape
bugCandidates.explanation: The peroxide is still there; the missing piece is a working enzyme. Heat denatured the catalase, not the peroxide.

bugCandidates.label: I forgot that denaturing changes shape, not the amino-acid sequence
bugCandidates.explanation: True and useful, but the central error is blaming the peroxide instead of the enzyme.

bugCandidates.label: I treated the enzyme as something that gets used up in the reaction
bugCandidates.explanation: Enzymes are reusable catalysts, but that is not why the boiled potato failed.

data.poweredIdea: Heat denatures enzymes — a changed shape means the substrate no longer fits.

data.prompt: An enzyme catalyzes its reaction fastest at its _____ temperature.
data.hint: The 'just right' temperature for that enzyme

achievement.flavor: You explain why an enzyme speeds a reaction without being used up — and why heat shuts it down.
